Jamaat’s New Challenge: A Prerequisite for Success—A Purge of Scandal-Prone and Opportunistic Elements!!

A review of the history of political and social organizations reveals a clear reality: when a party or organization grows strong through popular support, assumes state power, or comes close to the corridors of power, it does not attract only principled, self-sacrificing, and dedicated activists. At the same time, various opportunists, hypocrites, self-seeking individuals, and fair-weather supporters also seek to take shelter under its banner. For them, personal standing, influence, financial benefits, or a share in power often become more important than the organization’s ideology, objectives, and values.

It is not only new entrants who pose this risk. History also shows that even among long-serving, tested leaders and activists, some may lose their self-restraint when circumstances become favourable. After years of struggle, when prestige, influence, and various privileges come within reach, personal ambitions, the desire for positions, and self-interest may lead some of them astray. Consequently, the sacrifice and ideological commitment that once defined them gradually begin to fade.

This is not an exceptional problem unique to any particular organization; rather, it is a historical and sociological reality confronting almost all major organizations.

In this respect, Jamaat-e-Islami is not immune to such risks. Opportunistic, hypocritical, and self-seeking individuals may find their way into the party, while tendencies towards personal gain may also resurface among some of its long-standing leaders and activists. A realistic assessment of any organization requires that this possibility be acknowledged and considered carefully rather than denied.

History teaches another important lesson: when such tendencies within an organization move beyond isolated instances and begin to influence its organizational culture, the process of decline sets in. Personal loyalty begins to displace principle, flattery takes precedence over merit, nepotism replaces justice, and factional allegiance supplants accountability.

Ultimately, such elements have become a principal cause of internal weakness in many once-powerful organizations.

For this reason, self-criticism, accountability, and regular internal reform are not luxuries for any ideologically driven organization; they are among the essential conditions for its survival. An organization that can identify deviations early, establish the truth through impartial investigations, and take fair measures regardless of an individual’s identity or past contributions is more likely to remain stable in the long run.

Conversely, when irregularities, corruption, and opportunism are tolerated out of blind loyalty to individuals or factions, the organization’s moral foundations gradually erode, and public trust steadily diminishes.

In this context, it is worth recalling a divine pattern established by Allah Almighty. Whether in the case of individuals or societies, Allah does not generally punish someone immediately after the first transgression. Rather, He grants opportunities for reform and return. But when someone fails to take advantage of those opportunities and continues to transgress, Allah’s seizure comes so suddenly that the person could never have imagined it. Allah Almighty describes this reality in the Holy Qur’an:

﴿فَلَمَّا نَسُوا مَا ذُكِّرُوا بِهِ فَتَحْنَا عَلَيْهِمْ أَبْوَابَ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ حَتَّىٰ إِذَا فَرِحُوا بِمَا أُوتُوا أَخَذْنَاهُمْ بَغْتَةً فَإِذَا هُمْ مُّبْلِسُونَ﴾

“But when they forgot the admonition they had been given, We opened for them the gates of everything. Then, when they rejoiced in what they had been granted, We seized them suddenly, and they were left utterly despondent.” (Surah al-Anʿām, 6:44)

This verse teaches an important principle that applies to both individuals and societies. Outward success, power, influence, or prosperity does not necessarily indicate Allah’s pleasure; it may instead represent a period of respite granted to allow reform. If that opportunity becomes a cause of complacency, transgression, and moral decline rather than self-purification and correction, Allah’s seizure may come so unexpectedly that no one could have anticipated it.

Therefore, individuals and organizations alike should not become complacent over temporary success. Instead, they should continually strive to earn Allah’s pleasure through self-examination, accountability, and moral purification.

In this connection, an incident narrated from Anas ibn Mālik (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhu) is also noteworthy. When a thief was brought before ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhu), the man swore by Allah that it was his first theft. ʿUmar replied, “You are lying. Allah does not expose one of His servants in this manner for the very first offence.” (Abū Dāwūd)

In light of this principle, it may be said that an organization, too, does not usually face destruction at the very first sign of deviation. But if moral decline continues to deepen, accountability weakens, and opportunistic and corrupt elements gradually become more influential, then, in accordance with Allah’s established pattern, that organization may eventually face a severe trial.

Against the backdrop of various recent discussions, public reactions, and a number of isolated incidents, many observers have expressed concern that tendencies such as self-interest, opportunism, nepotism, regionalism, and loyalty centred on particular individuals or factions are becoming visible in Jamaat-e-Islami as well. Determining the validity of these assessments is, of course, the responsibility of the organization’s own institutional mechanisms.

Nevertheless, rather than dismissing the allegations outright, an ideologically committed organization should investigate them promptly and impartially, undertake effective reform where necessary through self-criticism, and ensure that organizational measures are taken fairly.

It hardly needs saying that the greatest strength of an ideological movement lies not in the size of its membership, but in its moral credibility.

If Jamaat-e-Islami can demonstrate the courage to engage in timely self-criticism, examine allegations impartially, take effective action against opportunistic and ideologically wayward elements, and place competence, *taqwā* (God-consciousness), accountability, and justice at the heart of its organizational culture, its social acceptance and long-term strength will be further consolidated.

But if the tendency to place personal and factional interests above ideology continues to grow, and deviations are neglected, then, as history has taught us about organizations of all kinds, the risk of moral decline and a crisis of public trust will continue to deepen.
